title: Semaglutide Dosage Chart: Understanding the Standard Titration Schedule
seo_title: Semaglutide Dosage Chart: Understanding the Standard Titration Schedule
meta_title: Semaglutide Dosage Chart & Titration Guide | WellPeps
meta_description: The standard semaglutide titration schedule explained week by week, why doses start low, how compounded dosing differs, and what dosing in units means.
lede_html:
If you’re starting semaglutide or researching treatment, one of the first questions most people have is simple: what dose will I take, and when does it change?

Semaglutide is not prescribed at a single fixed dose. Instead, healthcare providers typically follow a gradual step-up schedule called titration, where the dose starts low and increases slowly over several months. This approach gives your body time to adjust and may help reduce common side effects such as nausea.

This guide walks through the standard titration schedule used with FDA-approved semaglutide products, explains why the schedule looks the way it does, and covers two questions that come up constantly: why a compounded semaglutide schedule may look different, and what it means when a dose is described in “units.”

One important note before the chart: your prescribed schedule is the one that matters. The charts below describe general, publicly available prescribing frameworks for educational purposes — they are not instructions, and dosing should never be changed without guidance from your healthcare provider.
body_html:
The Standard Semaglutide Titration Schedule

For FDA-approved semaglutide products prescribed for chronic weight management, the published prescribing information describes a gradual monthly step-up. A typical schedule looks like this:

PhaseWeeksTypical weekly dose
Starting doseWeeks 1–40.25 mg
Step 2Weeks 5–80.5 mg
Step 3Weeks 9–121 mg
Step 4Weeks 13–161.7 mg
MaintenanceWeek 17 onward2.4 mg

A few things are worth understanding about this chart:

  • The 0.25 mg starting dose is an adjustment dose. It is not considered a treatment dose on its own — its purpose is to let your digestive system acclimate.
  • Each step typically lasts about four weeks, though providers may hold a dose longer if side effects need more time to settle.
  • Not everyone reaches the highest dose. Some people do well at an intermediate maintenance dose, and a provider may keep a patient at a lower step that is working.

Semaglutide products prescribed for type 2 diabetes follow a related but different schedule, with different maintenance doses. The right framework depends on the product, the indication, and the individual — which is why the schedule on your prescription label may not match a chart you find online.

Why Doses Start Low and Increase Gradually

Semaglutide slows stomach emptying and acts on appetite-regulation pathways. Starting at a full treatment dose would give the digestive system no time to adapt, which is why nausea, constipation, and stomach discomfort are most common in the first weeks and after dose increases.

Titration exists to manage this. By increasing the dose roughly every four weeks, the schedule gives your body a chance to adjust at each step before the next one. Many people find side effects are most noticeable for a few days after a step up, then ease.

If side effects are difficult at any step, tell your provider. Holding a dose steady for longer, or stepping back temporarily, is a routine part of how this medication is managed — not a failure of treatment.

Compounded Semaglutide: Why Your Chart May Look Different

Compounded semaglutide is prepared by licensed compounding pharmacies rather than the original manufacturer, and it is typically dispensed as a vial of liquid at a specific concentration rather than in a fixed-dose pen.

Because of that, a compounded prescription is individualized by the prescribing provider, and the schedule may differ from the chart above in several ways:

  • The provider may use different step sizes or hold phases longer, tailoring the escalation to how you respond.
  • Doses are often described as a volume to draw up (for example, in units on a syringe) rather than as a pen setting.
  • The concentration of the vial determines how much liquid corresponds to your prescribed dose — and concentrations vary between pharmacies and prescriptions.

This is why the only dosing instructions that apply to a compounded prescription are the ones on your label and from your provider. A chart built for one concentration can be wrong — and unsafe — for another.

What “Dosing in Units” Means

Compounded semaglutide is usually drawn up with an insulin-style syringe, which is marked in units. This causes a lot of confusion, so it’s worth being precise:

  • A unit on the syringe is a measure of volume, not a measure of semaglutide. On a standard U-100 insulin syringe, 100 units equal 1 mL of liquid.
  • How many milligrams of semaglutide are in that volume depends entirely on the concentration of your vial.
  • The same number of units can therefore contain very different amounts of medication from two different vials.

For exactly this reason, this guide does not include a units-to-milligrams conversion chart. Any such chart is only valid for one specific concentration, and following one that doesn’t match your vial could mean taking far too much or too little. Your pharmacy label and your provider’s instructions state the number of units for your prescription — those are the numbers to use, and your care team can walk you through drawing up a dose if you’re ever unsure.

Common Questions About the Schedule

What happens if I miss a dose?

The prescribing information for semaglutide products includes specific guidance on missed doses, and it depends on how close you are to your next scheduled dose. Rather than relying on a general rule, check your medication’s official instructions or contact your provider or pharmacist — they can tell you whether to take the missed dose or skip it based on your situation.

Can I stay at a lower dose if it’s working?

Possibly. Maintenance dosing is individualized, and some providers keep patients at an intermediate dose when it is well tolerated and working. This is a conversation to have with your provider at follow-up.

Can I speed up the schedule?

No — not on your own. Escalating faster than prescribed increases the likelihood of side effects, and dose changes should only ever come from your prescribing provider.

What about switching to tirzepatide?

Semaglutide and tirzepatide are different medications with different dosing frameworks, and there is no direct one-to-one conversion between them. If a switch is being considered, your provider will determine an appropriate starting dose of the new medication — usually not the top of its range.
key_takeaways:
• Semaglutide is prescribed on a gradual step-up (titration) schedule, typically increasing about every four weeks.
  • The low starting dose exists to reduce side effects while your body adjusts — it isn’t the treatment dose.
  • Compounded semaglutide schedules are individualized and often measured in syringe units, which are a volume — the milligrams depend on your vial’s concentration.
  • Never use a units conversion chart that wasn’t written for your exact prescription, and never change your dose without your provider.
cta_title: Questions About Your Dose? Start with a Real Medical Evaluation
cta_html: Every person’s health history, goals, and treatment needs are unique. If you’re considering weight management treatment, the licensed healthcare providers at WellPeps will review your health assessment, medical history, current medications, and wellness goals to determine whether treatment may be appropriate for you. If medically appropriate, they’ll recommend a personalized treatment plan — including a dosing schedule designed for you — and provide ongoing guidance throughout your care.
disclaimer_html: This article is provided for educational purposes only and should not be considered medical advice. It is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease, or replace consultation with a qualified healthcare professional. Individual treatment recommendations, including all dosing decisions, should always be made by a licensed healthcare provider based on your personal medical history, current health status, and individual healthcare needs.
